title: Redwood discovery - reliability & fallbacks with Cosmos Labs
transcript: 00:00 Jared Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Jared from Redwood - I'll run through high-level and Priya will join on the deep ops questions. 00:08 Anita Rao: Thanks Jared, appreciate it. We wanted to focus this session on reliability, incident tolerance, and fallback strategies - basically how Redwood behaves when things go sideways. 00:17 Jared Morales: Great. Quick agenda: current infra and pain points, expected SLAs, fallback options (model variants, routing), multi-region, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, and next steps. 00:30 Marcus Bell: Quick context - Cosmos Labs runs inference for a customer-facing chat assistant and a fraud-detector reranker. Traffic is bursty - big peaks during market hours, roughly 200-600 req/s for chat, 50-200 for rerank. Latency SLO is 150ms p95 for rerank and 300ms p95 for chat. We also have strict data residency and SOC2 requirements. 00:55 Priya Singh: Okay makes sense. On hosted vs dedicated: hosted gives fastest onboarding and simpler auto-failover across regions; dedicated gives you reserved capacity, control over GPU pools and slightly stronger isolation. For reliability, both support multi-region routing and policy-based fallbacks. 01:14 Anita Rao: Can you walk through a realistic failure scenario? Say a region goes down or a model crashes mid-generation. How does Redwood keep the application up? 01:25 Priya Singh: Sure. Typical policy is layered: first try same region same model, if capacity constrained or node failure, we have automatic routing to a warm regional replica; if that isn't available, we fall back to a compatible model variant - usually a lower-memory quantized variant or smaller architecture with validated output quality. If routing is exhausted, we escalate to a degraded response path - for chat that might be a cached prefix response or a shorter answer, and for reranker we return last-known-good ranking with an indicator. 01:56 Marcus Bell: How automatic is the routing - do we need to build client-side logic? 02:03 Priya Singh: Routing is server-side. You define a policy in the deployment config: priorities, acceptable latency window, and model variants. The SDK supports hints (region preference), but failover is handled by Redwood so your client remains simple. 02:16 Sana Iqbal: From a security/audit standpoint - when you route to another region, how do you handle data residency and encryption? Our policy forbids leaving EU data. 02:26 Priya Singh: For Private deployments we can keep traffic in-region always. For Hosted, we allow region-pin policies: you can mark requests as EU-only; if EU capacity isn't available, you can choose to fail closed or fail open to a certified region - but we'd surface that in an incident. We support KMS integration: customer-managed keys (CMKs) so data at rest is encrypted with your key, and audit logs record routing decisions. 02:49 Anita Rao: Good. Do you have SOC2 / ISO artifacts we can share with our auditors? 02:54 Jared Morales: Yes - we'll share the compliance pack. I'll put the link in the follow-up. 03:02 Owen Reed: On SLAs - what uptime/latency SLAs do you have for Hosted vs Dedicated? 03:07 Jared Morales: Hosted has a best-effort SLA for free tiers, paid tiers have more guarantees; Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets tied to reserved capacity agreements. Typical enterprise Dedicated SLA is 99.9% and latency SLOs are contractual based on capacity sizing. 03:23 Owen Reed: If there's an incident and we fall back to a smaller model, will output quality be tracked? We need to know when degraded answers are being served. 03:31 Priya Singh: Yes. We tag responses with model metadata and a degradation flag. Console shows per-model call ratios, fallback counts, and we can wire alerts when fallbacks exceed thresholds. Also you can route degraded calls to a special telemetry pipeline for more sampling. 03:48 Marcus Bell: Can we control the fallback threshold? Like only fall back if p95 latency > 400ms? 03:54 Priya Singh: Absolutely - policies are programmable: you can set latency thresholds, cost thresholds, or explicit capacity signals. You can also do gradual fallback - e.g., 10% of traffic to fallback model during overload to validate quality. 04:10 Anita Rao: Multi-region - does Redwood do active-active or active-passive? 04:15 Priya Singh: By default it's active-active with smart routing; we do health checks and latency-aware routing. For Private/On-Prem you can configure active-active or active-passive depending on WAN constraints. 04:26 Marcus Bell: What's the typical failover time if a region becomes unhealthy? 04:30 Priya Singh: Health checks are sub-10s; routing changes are propagated in under 30s in Hosted, assuming no control-plane partition. Per-request KV caches are warmed - there can be a short cache miss penalty. We recommend warm-replicas for <60s recovery. 04:45 Anita Rao: You mentioned KV cache - how does that behave across regions? 04:49 Priya Singh: Prefix KV cache is per-runtime. In multi-region you can set cache affinity - either keep regional caches (so lower latency) or replicate critical prefixes to global caches for faster warmups. Replication increases cost and complexity. 05:03 Marcus Bell: For our fraud reranker, consistency matters - we can't have divergent ranks during failover. 05:10 Priya Singh: Understood. For rerankers we support sticky sessions and state pinning to GPU pools; if exact consistency is required, recommended pattern is to run active-passive with synchronous replication of ranker state or ship deterministic reranker logic to the client as a fallback. 05:27 Anita Rao: About observability - what logs/trace granularity do you expose during incidents? 05:33 Jared Morales: We expose token-level latency breakdowns, per-route traces, and routing decision logs. Audit logs include which model variant served each request and why a fallback occurred. You can forward logs to your SIEM. 05:47 Sana Iqbal: Are audit logs tamper-evident? 05:50 Priya Singh: We support write-once storage options and can ingest logs into your KMS-backed storage; we also provide cryptographic hashes on log batches for tamper evidence as an add-on. 06:05 Marcus Bell: In terms of capacity - how do you recommend sizing Dedicated versus Hosted for our peaks? 06:11 Priya Singh: For predictable peaks, Dedicated makes unit economics better because you reserve GPU pools sized to your p95 throughput. Hosted is better if peaks are spiky and unpredictable because we can autoscale, but that may have higher variability in latency or cost. 06:25 Anita Rao: Do you support burst capacity on Dedicated for unexpected traffic? 06:29 Priya Singh: Yes - burst contracts let Dedicated customers exceed reserved capacity for short windows. Bursts are billed at a premium but avoid hard throttling. 06:38 Owen Reed: Can you run canary rollouts and automatic rollback if quality regressions are detected? 06:43 Priya Singh: Yes - rollouts are first-class. You can configure canary percentages, automatic rollback triggers (based on latency, token-quality metrics, or eval test failures), and A/B experiments. 06:56 Marcus Bell: Suppose an incident affects only the model itself - e.g., a buggy forward pass in a new version - what's the recovery path? 07:04 Priya Singh: We'll route to the last-known-good pinned model variant instantly. If that variant isn't compatible we can spin up a hot-standby with a different quantization profile. We also support pinned KV caches per model version to avoid cold start regressions. 07:22 Anita Rao: How do you validate that fallback models maintain acceptable business metrics? 07:27 Priya Singh: We recommend preflight evals - Redwood Optimize can run your prompt set against candidate fallback models and produce delta reports on quality metrics. We also support canary loads and sample-by-sample ground truth scoring. 07:40 Owen Reed: For privacy, can we ensure tokens never leave our VPC? 07:44 Priya Singh: In Private deployments yes - the control plane can be customer-managed and the data plane sits inside your VPC. For Hosted, we offer VPC peering options and private link like setups so data traverses private links. 07:56 Sana Iqbal: What about encryption in transit to GPUs? 08:00 Priya Singh: TLS and mTLS are supported end-to-end. For extra measures on Dedicated/Private we can run GPU hosts with encrypted NVLink segments where supported by hardware partners, but that's an advanced option. 08:15 Marcus Bell: On incident communication - will we get real-time status updates and a postmortem? 08:19 Jared Morales: Yes - enterprise customers get an incident channel, proactive paging, and an SLA-compliant postmortem with timeline and remediation items. 08:28 Anita Rao: What's your RTO/RPO targets for Dedicated? 08:32 Jared Morales: RTO targets are in the minutes-to-1-hour range depending on the incident severity, documented in the SLA. RPO depends on workload - for stateless text generation RPO is near-zero; for stateful caches we recommend replication to meet your RPO needs. 08:47 Marcus Bell: Are there examples or runbooks we can review for common incidents? 08:51 Priya Singh: Yes - we'll share runbooks for node failures, model OOMs, and network partitions. 08:57 Anita Rao: Ok digging into a few nitty-gritty - model quantization: if a fallback is quantized, do you see hallucination or format changes? 09:06 Priya Singh: In general smaller or quantized models can affect generation style; that's why we prefer to validate fallback models with your evals. We also add a post-processing layer to maintain formatting. There can be subtle differences, so we recommend surfacing fallbacks to users or providing a confidence flag. 09:28 Owen Reed: Cost controls - can we limit when failovers to a larger, more expensive region happen? 09:34 Priya Singh: Yes, policy can include cost budgets: e.g., only route to global region if budget bucket has room, otherwise fail closed or route to cheaper model. 09:44 Marcus Bell: Let's talk throttling and graceful degradation - do you do circuit breaker patterns? 09:49 Priya Singh: We do. You can define circuit-breakers per route that degrade responses progressively - from full answers to shorter answers to cached responses. Circuit states are visible in Console. 10:00 Anita Rao: If we need to certify behavior for auditors, can you provide test harnesses to simulate region outage and show routing logs? 10:07 Priya Singh: Yes - we'll provide a simulation harness and we can run a controlled failover with you. 10:13 Owen Reed: Timeline question - we want to run a 6-week POC that includes a resilience test. Is that feasible? 10:19 Jared Morales: Yep - standard POC is 4-8 weeks. We'll size Dedicated or Hosted capacity for the POC depending on your requirements. 10:27 Marcus Bell: Who else on our side needs to be involved? 10:30 Anita Rao: Platform and security - Marcus and Sana - and Product for acceptance - Owen. 10:35 Jared Morales: Great. Next steps we'll outline in the follow-up. 10:39 Priya Singh: Quick note on monitoring: we emit metrics to Prometheus and can send traces to Jaeger/Zipkin; you can also pull per-token latency histograms. 10:50 Marcus Bell: For our reranker we'll want end-to-end determinism tests. 10:54 Priya Singh: We'll include a test template. 11:00 Owen Reed: One more - if there's a legal/data request related to routed data in a fallback region, who owns notifications? 11:07 Jared Morales: For Hosted, Redwood will notify per contract; for Private, it's customer-managed. We'll include notification obligations in the SRA. 11:20 Anita Rao: Ok let's recap, please correct me if I miss anything. 11:25 Marcus Bell: We discussed routing layers, failover to warm replicas, fallbacks to model variants, active-active vs active-passive, per-region KV cache strategies, policy-driven thresholds (latency/cost), Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, burst capacity, canary rollouts with automatic rollback, observability/audit logs, KMS/CAC integration, and compliance artifacts. 11:46 Jared Morales: Perfect. I'll send the compliance pack, runbooks, pricing guidance for Dedicated burst contracts, and a POC proposal with a resilience test plan. 12:00 Anita Rao: We'll schedule an ops deep-dive next week if that works. 12:06 Owen Reed: Yes, we can do a deep dive on reranker determinism. 12:12 Jared Morales: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the links and action items. 12:18 END
summary: Discovery focused on incident tolerance and routing policies. Discussed layered failover (warm replicas, model variants, degraded responses), multi-region active-active and active-passive modes, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, SLAs and incident comms, observability and audit logs, KMS and data residency, canary rollouts and automatic rollback, cache strategies, and recommended POC with resilience tests.
